checkpoints.prompt: A developer needs to run a short transformation only when a file arrives in S3. Choose one way to run it without the team managing the OS.

choices.text: Run Lambda in response to an S3 event
choices.explanation: This enables event-driven processing without managing a server OS.

choices.text: Manually log in to EC2 and run it
choices.explanation: Manual OS operations do not meet the requirements.

choices.text: Use S3 as the execution environment
choices.explanation: S3 is a storage service.

choices.text: Save commands in DynamoDB
choices.explanation: DynamoDB is not a command execution environment.

checkpoints.title: Compute: Who manages the execution environment

checkpoints.prompt: A developer needs multiple processes to read the same image using a key corresponding to its file name. It does not need to be connected as an OS disk. Choose one storage destination that meets the requirements.

choices.text: Store it as an S3 object
choices.explanation: The shared image can be handled using a key.

choices.text: Copy it to each EC2 instance’s EBS
choices.explanation: Managing individual copies will be necessary.

choices.text: Store it only in Lambda’s temporary storage
choices.explanation: This is not a persistent shared storage destination.

choices.text: Always split and store it in RDS
choices.explanation: An RDB is not required for image storage.

checkpoints.title: Storage: Object or attached disk

checkpoints.prompt: A developer searches orders by customer ID and date and joins multiple tables. Transactions are required for simultaneous updates to orders and details. Choose one service to consider first.

choices.text: Consider RDS and verify the relational requirements
choices.explanation: Joins and transactions are the comparison criteria.

choices.text: Always choose DynamoDB without reviewing the requirements
choices.explanation: Choose DynamoDB after verifying the key design.

choices.text: Join using only S3 file names
choices.explanation: S3 does not provide relational joins.

choices.text: Make EBS a shared database directly across multiple AZs
choices.explanation: EBS does not provide database query capabilities.

checkpoints.title: Database: Choose based on the queries

checkpoints.prompt: An e-commerce development team is designing functions to store and transform product images and to let staff search orders. Choose two appropriate ways to divide responsibilities for image storage and order searches, respectively.

choices.text: Assign image storage to S3 objects
choices.explanation: Images can be stored and retrieved by key.

choices.text: Compare order searches against the requirements for RDS or DynamoDB
choices.explanation: Use search characteristics as input for database selection.

choices.text: Consolidate all requirements into manually managed files on EBS
choices.explanation: This ignores the difference between storage formats and queries.

choices.text: Perform image transformation using only database search functionality
choices.explanation: Transformation is a computing responsibility.

checkpoints.title: Combination: Break Requirements Down into Responsibilities

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Break down the requirements for compute, storage, and retrieval, then choose among EC2, Lambda, S3, EBS, RDS, and DynamoDB.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Select AWS services based on compute, storage, and data characteristics.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Choose an execution method based on execution time and whether OS management is required.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Distinguish between object storage and attached disks.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Compare databases based on joins, transactions, and key-based access.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Break down multiple responsibilities into a combination of services.

blocks.label: Compute: Who manages the execution environment
blocks.text: EC2 is a virtual server that lets users manage the OS and installed software. It is a candidate when requirements include resident software, long-running processes, or OS configuration.

blocks.label: Compute: Who manages the execution environment
blocks.text: Lambda is a service that runs code in response to events, and users do not manage the server OS. Choose it after checking the processing time, concurrency, and trigger.

steps.label: Compute: Who manages the execution environment

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Run a short resizing process only when an image arrives in S3.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Use the arrival event as the trigger.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check Lambda's processing time and retries.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: If OS residency is required, compare with EC2.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Can distinguish event-driven processing from processing that requires OS management.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Putting a file in S3 makes S3 execute the transformation command.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: S3 is a storage service. Assign transformations to execution environments such as Lambda or EC2.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: For event-driven processing that reduces OS management, compare Lambda.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: If resident software or OS management is required, compare EC2.

blocks.label: Storage: objects or attached disks
blocks.text: S3 is an object storage service that handles images, documents, and other items by key. It is suitable for source files and outputs shared by name across multiple processes.

blocks.label: Storage: objects or attached disks
blocks.text: EBS is block storage attached to EC2 and is used for operating system file systems and similar purposes. Lambda’s temporary storage is not a persistent shared storage location.

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: Store the EC2 operating system area and users’ uploaded images separately.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Consider EBS for the operating system area.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Consider S3 objects for the image data.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check the key, retention period, and access principal.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Do not confuse attached disks with shared objects.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: You can manage access by storing all data in IAM.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: IAM provides access control; it is not a storage location for images or documents.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: S3 is object storage accessed by key.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: EBS is block storage attached to EC2.

blocks.label: Database: Choose Based on Query Patterns
blocks.text: RDS is a service for operating relational databases, evaluated based on table relationships, SQL, joins, and transactions.

blocks.label: Database: Choose Based on Query Patterns
blocks.text: DynamoDB is a key-value database in which access patterns and key design are determined first. Verify which keys will be used for reads and writes and whether the required queries fit.

steps.label: Database: Choose Based on Query Patterns

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Join customers, orders, and order items to produce a monthly aggregate.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: List the required joins and integrity requirements.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Compare the SQL requirements with RDS as a candidate.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: If key access is central, also compare DynamoDB against the separate requirements.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Choose based on query and operational requirements, not on the service name.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: With DynamoDB, joins on arbitrary columns can be automatically optimized later.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: DynamoDB prioritizes access patterns and key design and does not assume arbitrary joins.

blocks.label: Key points
blocks.text: Joins, SQL, and transactions are comparison criteria for RDS.

blocks.label: Key points
blocks.text: Key access and query patterns are comparison criteria for DynamoDB.

blocks.label: Decomposition: Break requirements into roles
blocks.text: Even a single feature can involve distinct responsibilities: receiving, storing, transforming, and searching. Compare the execution model, data shape, queries, and permission boundaries for each responsibility separately.

blocks.label: Decomposition: Break requirements into roles
blocks.text: Assign services to roles—for example, store images in S3, invoke Lambda when an arrival event occurs, and register order information in RDS or DynamoDB.

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Receive and inspect a CSV, register business data, and retain the original.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Store the original as an S3 object.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Compare Lambda or EC2 based on the inspection trigger and processing time.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Choose a database based on search and consistency.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Explain the reasons for the service selection and the permission boundaries.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Choose one familiar service first and fit the requirements to it afterward.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: First separate the responsibilities for processing, storage, and search, then choose a combination that meets the requirements.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Treat receiving, storage, transformation, and search as separate responsibilities.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Verify the service selection and permission boundary together.
